main.title: PlayStation
main.subtitle: Changing the material changed the possibilities
main.summary: Sony's first PlayStation joined real-time polygons to the capacity of a CD, giving developers new choices about what a console game could contain.

cards.heading: A familiar disc, a new console
cards.text: Open the lid and the change is easy to recognise. A PlayStation game sits on a compact disc, an object already familiar from recorded music. Sony launched the console in Japan on 3 December 1994; North America and Europe followed in September 1995. The format helped make room for more recorded sound, imagery and video, alongside the worlds being drawn in real time.

cards.heading: Space for sound and images
cards.text: That capacity was a practical decision for developers as well as a selling point for players. Sony's history of the machine emphasises that CDs could hold more data than cartridge alternatives and could be manufactured more quickly and affordably. Games with large amounts of art and music, including Final Fantasy VII, could be built around those possibilities.

cards.heading: Choosing a visual language
cards.text: Real-time polygons gave racing games three-dimensional circuits and moving viewpoints. Adventures could combine pre-rendered scenes with animated characters, while recorded video provided another way to stage dramatic sequences. Developers chose between these techniques according to the needs of a scene, drawing on both the console's graphics hardware and the capacity of its discs.

cards.heading: The objects around the machine
cards.text: The objects around the console also tell the story. A memory card held progress that could leave the machine, and the same disc drive could play an audio CD. PlayStation connected gaming with a wider household culture of music, screens and collected media. Its significance lies in the range of experiences that teams built from that combination.

cards.heading: The international launch
cards.text: Sony Computer Entertainment launched PlayStation in North America on September 9, 1995, following its Japanese debut nine months earlier. Europe followed twenty days later. Ridge Racer and Tekken brought recognisable three-dimensional arcade experiences to the home, helping establish the new platform. The console's expansion also depended on its controllers, Memory Cards, audio capabilities and growing development network. PlayStation would eventually surpass one hundred million units sold.

cards.heading: From collaboration to an independent platform
cards.text: Sony's work with Nintendo on a CD-ROM system for the Super Famicom preceded the first PlayStation. When that collaboration failed to produce the intended machine, Ken Kutaragi continued to support a Sony platform designed for three-dimensional graphics. Sony's historical account records doubts within the company about entering video games. Developing an independent console meant establishing relationships with game developers and distributors alongside the hardware itself.

cards.heading: Making and distributing discs
cards.text: CD-ROM changed the economics of publishing games. Compared with cartridges, discs offered more storage, faster duplication and lower manufacturing costs. Publishers could include larger quantities of audio, video and artwork, and replenish retail stock more quickly. Sony's corporate history also describes a more direct route to Japanese retailers. These manufacturing and distribution choices helped support a library ranging from arcade conversions to narrative games spread across several discs.

cards.heading: Building games in three dimensions
cards.text: PlayStation's 32-bit R3000 processor and graphics hardware were designed for the shift toward real-time three-dimensional games. Characters could be built from polygons, cameras could move through scenes, and tracks could stretch into the distance. Ridge Racer and Tekken provided clear early demonstrations. As more developers worked in 3D, camera placement, movement and orientation became important design problems for home games.

cards.heading: The controller and its four symbols
cards.text: The original controller retained a directional pad and added two grips. Its four face buttons used triangle, circle, cross and square in place of letters. Designer Teiyu Goto described the shapes as simple, immediately recognisable icons. They became part of PlayStation's visual identity across games and menus. The first controller had no analogue sticks; later models developed its controls while preserving the familiar grips and symbols.

cards.heading: Progress on a Memory Card
cards.text: Many PlayStation games stored progress on a Memory Card inserted into one of the console's two front slots. Players could take their saves to a friend's house or replace a full card with another. Menus presented the available space as blocks and offered ways to copy or delete files. A collection of characters, completed stages or saved campaigns could therefore travel separately from both the disc and the console.

cards.heading: A growing library and audience
cards.text: PlayStation gained considerable attention at E3 before its North American launch in September 1995. Its growing library brought Ridge Racer and Tekken together with WipEout, followed by Resident Evil, Tomb Raider, Final Fantasy VII, Gran Turismo and Metal Gear Solid. Music, fashion, digital cinema and club culture also featured in the platform's public image. This variety helped Sony address an audience extending beyond the established image of the home-console player.

features.title: A shape becomes familiar
features.summary: The first PlayStation established shapes and colours that Sony returned to thirty years later.

cards.heading: A circle in a rectangle
cards.text: The first PlayStation placed a round disc lid inside a rectangular case. Sony's institutional history identifies this arrangement as part of the machine's visual identity. The circle showed players where the disc belonged, and opening the lid became a familiar part of starting a game. The console's simple exterior gave a visible place to the storage format at the centre of its design.

cards.heading: An identity held in the hands
cards.text: Teiyu Goto designed the controller's grips and its four geometric face-button symbols. Triangle, circle, cross and square could be recognised quickly in a game's instructions and then found under the player's fingers. As those same signs appeared across the platform, they became associated with PlayStation itself. The controller joined a distinctive shape to a consistent set of controls.

cards.heading: The old palette meets new hardware
cards.text: In September 2024, Hideaki Nishino introduced anniversary products using the original PlayStation's colour scheme on PS5 consoles and DualSense controllers. The announcement connected this new hardware to the December 1994 launch. Grey surfaces and familiar coloured symbols allowed players to recognise the first machine in products built three decades later.

cards.heading: A connector becomes a keepsake
cards.text: The anniversary console bundles also included a cable connector housing styled after the original PlayStation controller. Cable ties reproduced the platform's symbols. These accessories extended the anniversary design beyond the console and controller to the smaller objects used when connecting and arranging a machine. The same shapes could remain recognisable at several different scales.

main.title: Uniracers
main.subtitle: One wheel, no rider
main.summary: Uniracers is DMA Design’s unusual Super Nintendo racing game about unicycles that need nobody to ride them. Released in Europe as Unirally, it sends the animated machines along two-dimensional tracks filled with loops, jumps and abrupt changes of direction. Performing a stunt increases speed, so acrobatics are part of racing well rather than an optional flourish. The player must turn a brief moment in the air into an advantage and still land safely enough to carry that extra pace into the next section.

cards.heading: One wheel, no rider
cards.text: Uniracers is DMA Design’s unusual Super Nintendo racing game about unicycles that need nobody to ride them. Released in Europe as Unirally, it sends the animated machines along two-dimensional tracks filled with loops, jumps and abrupt changes of direction. Performing a stunt increases speed, so acrobatics are part of racing well rather than an optional flourish. The player must turn a brief moment in the air into an advantage and still land safely enough to carry that extra pace into the next section.

cards.heading: A good landing is acceleration
cards.text: Stunts involve jumping and rotating around different axes. Completing one cleanly rewards the unicycle with speed, while landing badly causes a crash and loses the momentum already earned. The decision is therefore about how much can fit into the available space. A generous jump permits a longer combination; a low or crowded section demands restraint. Track markings provide information about what lies ahead, including shortcuts and hazards. Learning those visual signals helps the player prepare a stunt before the unicycle reaches the next take-off.

cards.heading: Race, circuit or performance
cards.text: The forty-five tracks are grouped into nine tours, with races, circuits and stunt events giving the same controls different objectives. Two-player split-screen play supports direct competition, and a league mode can organise several people into one-on-one races. The unicycles can also be named and retain individual progress. Those features give the small cast of differently coloured machines a social identity without introducing riders. Uniracers builds its personality from their movement: a good run looks playful because every successful trick is also useful to the race.

main.title: Beyond Oasis / The Story of Thor
main.subtitle: An adventure carried by four spirits
main.summary: Ancient’s action RPG first reached the Japanese Mega Drive on December 9, 1994, as The Story of Thor. Its young hero discovers a golden armlet that can summon four spirits, opening an adventure shaped by their different powers. Seen from above, the world mixes towns, outdoor routes and enclosed dungeons. Sword fighting shares the stage with running, jumping and interacting with the environment: running, jumping and interacting with objects help solve its rooms. Beyond Oasis is the North American name for this same original game.

cards.heading: The power of the golden armlet

Beyond Oasis is the North American name for this same original game.

cards.heading: Fighting, exploring, summoning
cards.text: The spirits expand what the hero can do, helping with both enemies and obstacles. Exploration therefore depends on recognising where a supernatural ability can change a seemingly ordinary place, alongside choosing weapons and managing supplies. The manual gives physical actions and equipment their own detailed explanations, reinforcing the connection between combat and navigation. Ancient, also known for Streets of Rage 2, pairs this energetic adventure with Yuzo Koshiro’s score.

main.title: Clockwork Knight
main.subtitle: Midnight in the toy room
main.summary: Clockwork Knight is Sega's platform game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 9 December 1994.

cards.heading: Midnight in the toy room
cards.text: Clockwork Knight is Sega's platform game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 9 December 1994. Pepper, a small toy knight, sets out to rescue Chelsea, whose voice brings the household's toys to life at midnight. The adventure takes him through rooms where ordinary furniture and possessions become enormous obstacles. Pre-rendered characters move through polygonal environments, with fully three-dimensional bosses adding another scale to the encounters. As one of Saturn's earliest games, it used this mixture to give a familiar side-scrolling journey the appearance of a miniature toy world.

cards.heading: A key with several uses
cards.text: Pepper's key provides his main attack. A quick thrust can stun an enemy, while repeated input twists the key into a more dangerous spinning motion. Stunned opponents and loose objects can also be lifted and thrown, including upwards. A nearby item may therefore become a weapon or a tool for reaching another part of the room. The player must judge jumps and deal with enemies before time or health runs out. Dying returns Pepper to the beginning of the level, making a successful route worth remembering.

cards.heading: Ordinary rooms at another scale
cards.text: The stages pass through children's bedrooms, a kitchen and an attic, with side areas offering treasures away from the direct route. Household objects supply the scenery and the obstacles, keeping Pepper's small size central to the adventure. Collected crowns can pay for continues or be risked in a bonus game after certain bosses. Hirofumi Murasaki's music accompanies the theatrical setting. The combination gives each room the character of a place already inhabited by toys, where a discarded object can become part of a knight's dangerous nighttime expedition.

main.title: Tekken
main.summary: Tekken is a 1994 fighting game developed and published by Namco.

cards.text: Tekken is a 1994 fighting game developed and published by Namco. It was originally released on arcades, then ported to the PlayStation home console in 1995. One of the earliest 3D polygon-based games of the genre, Tekken was Namco's answer to Virtua Fighter and was designed by Seiichi Ishii, who himself was also the game's designer when he worked at Sega previously. The game was developed on the purpose-built low-cost System 11 board, based on PlayStation hardware.

Plotwise, the game revolves around a tournament set up by Heihachi Mishima, who attempts to prove his power to his revenge-seeking son and protagonist, Kazuya. Tekken initially divided opinion regarding its presentation, character designs and unusual control system, which consisted of one button per limb. However, following its home console port originally released in March 1995 — only the third 3D console fighter following Virtua Fighter and Battle Arena Toshinden — it quickly rose in popularity and eventually became a PlayStation best seller based on copies sold, even quickly surpassing its two fighting game rivals. It started the Tekken series, with a sequel, Tekken 2, coming later in 1995. On June 25, 2026, the arcade version of the game got ported for modern consoles as part of the Arcade Archives 2 series.

main.title: Mega Man X2
main.subtitle: The dash is there from the start
main.summary: On December 16, 1994, Capcom released Rockman X2 in Japan, later distributed in the West as Mega Man X2, for Super Famicom and Super Nintendo.

cards.heading: X returns with a faster starting point
cards.text: Capcom released Rockman X2 in Japan on December 16, 1994, for Super Famicom, with Western versions titled Mega Man X2. The sequel gives X the ground dash from the beginning. Armour upgrades add further abilities, including an air dash, while optional encounters with the X-Hunters can change Zero's fate. A Cx4 coprocessor inside the cartridge supplies additional graphical effects.

cards.heading: From ground dash to air dash
cards.text: In the first Mega Man X, the player acquires the dash through an upgrade. X2 makes that movement available immediately and adds an air dash through its armour system. X can adjust his path in midair or reach more distant platforms. Capcom's official retrospective highlighted this progression: the sequel builds its obstacles around the faster movement players had learned in the first game.

cards.heading: Rebuilding Zero
cards.text: Violen, Serges and Agile appear during the campaign carrying parts of Zero's body. Defeating these X-Hunters allows the player to rebuild X's ally; leaving them undefeated changes later events and can lead to a confrontation with Zero. Choosing a stage therefore also involves checking where the X-Hunters have appeared and deciding whether to pursue an additional encounter.

cards.heading: The Cx4 inside the cartridge
cards.text: The Cx4 coprocessor sits inside the game cartridge and assists the Super Nintendo with graphics calculations. Rotation, scaling and wireframe effects give particular bosses, objects and sequences a distinctive appearance within the side-scrolling game. Rockman X2 and its Western releases use this supplementary hardware to add effects beyond those produced by the console alone.

main.title: Lunar: Eternal Blue
main.subtitle: A visitor from the Blue Star
main.summary: Lunar: Eternal Blue is Game Arts and Studio Alex's role-playing sequel, first released for Mega-CD in Japan on 22 December 1994.

cards.heading: A visitor from the Blue Star
cards.text: Lunar: Eternal Blue is Game Arts and Studio Alex's role-playing sequel, first released for Mega-CD in Japan on 22 December 1994. A thousand years after The Silver Star, the explorer Hiro meets Lucia, a visitor from the distant Blue Star seeking to prevent a catastrophe. Their journey gathers companions and brings them into conflict with Zophar. Towns, dungeons and turn-based encounters again provide the structure, while more elaborate animation and extensive spoken dialogue make fuller use of the disc hardware to present the cast and its changing relationships.

cards.heading: Preparing the party’s next move
cards.text: Combat builds on the original's use of distance, requiring characters to approach a target or attack from range. The player can arrange the party's starting positions, giving a chance to prepare for the next exchange before commands are carried out. Experience improves the characters' strength, while separate magical progression expands their abilities. The arrangement connects preparation to the visible action: choosing where a companion begins can influence how quickly that fighter reaches an enemy, and the party's growing repertoire offers more answers to the creatures encountered along the route.

cards.heading: A thousand years later
cards.text: Noriyuki Iwadare's music supports a world that carries the earlier adventure as history, allowing the sequel to revisit familiar ideas through another generation of characters. Working Designs' North American release followed in September 1995, with a localised script that emphasised the companions' personalities and humour. Later remakes changed the presentation again, but the original already pushed the Mega-CD's storytelling ambitions further. Its combination of longer animated sequences, voices and party-based encounters gave Hiro and Lucia's journey a sense of continuity between the scenes watched and the decisions made during exploration.

main.title: Comix Zone
main.subtitle: The page becomes the battlefield
main.summary: Comix Zone, released for the Mega Drive in 1995, makes the comic page part of the action. Sketch Turner, a New York artist, is drawn into his own work after lightning brings the villain Mortus to life. Mortus wants to destroy his creator and become real; General Alissa Cyan helps Sketch navigate the world inside the panels. The premise is visible throughout the game: frames organise the screen, speech balloons belong to the action, and moving between panels becomes part of progressing through the story. The Japanese Mega Drive edition followed on September 1, 1995.

cards.heading: Fighting through the frame
cards.text: Sega’s action game asks the player to read the page while fighting through it. A panel can contain enemies, an obstacle or an object worth examining; moving between frames is part of progressing through the level. Sketch’s punches and kicks turn the drawn world into a physical place, while changes of panel give the action its own rhythm. The original manual credits Peter Morawiec with concept, design and art direction, Adrian Stephens with technical direction and programming, and Howard Drossin with music and sound effects. Drossin’s score gives this paper world a distinctly forceful musical voice.

main.title: Cyber Troopers Virtual-On
main.summary: Two control sticks turn running, jumping and firing into a high-speed duel between robots with very different weapons.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Cyber Troopers Virtual-On is Sega AM3's original Model 2 robot-combat game from 1995, followed by a Saturn version in 1996. Two Virtuaroids fight across a 3D arena viewed from behind the player's machine. Hajime Katoki's robot designs give the roster distinct shapes, while the twin-stick controls make movement a central part of learning each one.

cards.heading: Move both sticks, move the machine
cards.text: The two sticks work together rather than simply controlling two separate weapons. Their combinations produce movement, turning and jumping, with buttons adding dashes and attacks. A jump also helps bring the opponent back into view, but leaving the ground gives the rival another movement to read. The player keeps adjusting position and facing, trying to make a weapon useful while preventing the other machine from lining up its own shot.

cards.heading: Leave an opening after the shot
cards.text: Left, right and centre weapons have separate energy supplies, and using them too freely can leave one unavailable until it recharges. Firing while dashing or jumping changes an attack's behaviour, but a dash also has an ending that an opponent can anticipate. The useful question becomes what follows a shot. A powerful attack that misses may expose the machine, while a smaller one can keep pressure on the rival without spending every option at once.

cards.heading: Read the distance to the rival
cards.text: Distance changes the encounter again. Move close enough and the lock-on indicates that weapons can become melee attacks, replacing a long-range exchange with a more immediate clash. Arena structures offer cover, but staying behind one gives the opponent time to reposition. The roster's different weapons turn those spaces into different opportunities. Learning a machine means discovering where it can threaten the rival most effectively, then using movement to create that distance before the next exchange begins.

main.title: Donald in Maui Mallard
main.subtitle: A detective with a ninja alter ego
main.summary: Donald in Maui Mallard first appeared on the European Mega Drive in 1995. Disney Interactive cast Donald as an island detective searching for the missing Shabuhm Shabuhm idol, with an unexpected second identity: the ninja Cold Shadow. One form uses a gun that fires insects; the other fights with a staff. Haunted places, pirates and fantastical enemies surround a hero whose costume and movement change with his abilities. The combination makes the familiar duck a character built around two different ways of tackling a platform adventure.

cards.heading: Animation, synthesis and different editions
cards.text: Artist Oliver Wade described polishing the hand-drawn animation and its transitions, while composer and sound designer Patrick J. Collins explained adapting Michael Giacchino’s musical ideas to the Mega Drive’s FM sound. Collins even recreated bird calls through programmed pitch bends. He worked on the Sega and PC versions; Eurocom handled the later Super Nintendo adaptation. The game was known in North America as Maui Mallard in Cold Shadow.
